steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing the Recap, Deliberate, and Respond (RDR) method, a training pipeline meant to give NLU models more genuine language understanding using paraphrasing and external knowledge graphs. Cover the motivation, the method, and how we evaluate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: NLU models need context beyond the input; knowledge graphs as extra context
- Problem: models can game NLU benchmarks; existing mitigations fall short
- Our proposal: the RDR paradigm (Recap, Deliberate, Respond)
- Evaluation on GLUE tasks and main findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background: context beyond the input
  - prior NLU / neural pipeline work: need context beyond input data
  - established fix: integrate external knowledge graphs as supplementary context
  - KGs = structured info on entities, relationships, concepts
  - lets network infer semantic connections between entities even when not explicit in data -> uncovers implicit/missing associations
- Problem: benchmark gaming
  - prior research: NLU benchmarks vulnerable to manipulation by neural models
  - casts doubt on reliability, generalizability of reported metrics; heavily scrutinized in NLU community
  - mitigations: more comprehensive evaluation protocols, adversarial testing, integrating external knowledge into training
  - first two don't redesign training pipeline
  - knowledge integration modifies training, but unclear if knowledge factually and sufficiently enforced
- Our proposal: RDR paradigm, three objectives in the pipeline
  - Recap: paraphrase input with dedicated model -> essential, salient info
  - Deliberate: encode external graph info about entities in input; graph embedding model; better comprehension of entity relationships, extract relevant info for downstream tasks
  - Respond: classification head on Recap + Deliberate representations -> final prediction, more accurate/informed
  - cascading structure + minimizing combined loss -> prevents inflating metrics via statistical artifacts
  - captures true semantic patterns with help of external knowledge -> more reliable predictions
- Evaluation
  - multiple GLUE tasks: sentence similarity, textual entailment, NLI
  - beats competitive baselines, up to 2% on standard metrics
  - inference examples -> discuss robustness against statistical artifacts
  - Recap + Deliberate -> better comprehension of semantic patterns in data and external knowledge

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Previous work on natural language understanding (NLU) and neural network pipelines has recognized that models need more context than just the input data. One well-established way to deal with this is to add external knowledge graphs as extra context. Knowledge graphs hold structured information about entities, relationships, and concepts. With this external information the neural network can infer semantic connections between entities, even if those relations are not stated explicitly in the data itself. So the network is able to find implicit or missing contextual associations.

However, previous research has also raised a concern that NLU benchmarks are vulnerable to being manipulated by neural models. This makes it doubtful whether the performance metrics that neural models report on benchmark datasets are reliable and generalizable, and the NLU community has looked at this issue a lot. Researchers have tried different methods to reduce benchmark gaming so that NLU models show real language understanding. These include more comprehensive evaluation protocols, adversarial testing, and integrating external knowledge into training. But the first two do not change the training pipeline to make the model's language understanding better. The knowledge integration method does change the training procedure, but it is not clear whether the external knowledge is factually and sufficiently enforced in the integration.

- Our proposal: RDR paradigm, three objectives in the pipeline
  - Recap: paraphrase input with dedicated model -> essential, salient info
  - Deliberate: encode external graph info about entities in input; graph embedding model; better comprehension of entity relationships
  - Respond: classification head on Recap + Deliberate representations -> final prediction
  - cascading structure + combined loss -> no inflating metrics via statistical artifacts
- Evaluation
  - multiple GLUE tasks: sentence similarity, textual entailment, NLI
  - beats competitive baselines, up to 2% on standard metrics
  - inference examples -> robustness against statistical artifacts
  - Recap + Deliberate -> better comprehension of semantic patterns

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Previous work on natural language understanding (NLU) and neural network pipelines has recognized that models need more context than just the input data. One well-established way to deal with this is to add external knowledge graphs as extra context. Knowledge graphs hold structured information about entities, relationships, and concepts. With this external information the neural network can infer semantic connections between entities, even if those relations are not stated explicitly in the data itself. So the network is able to find implicit or missing contextual associations.

However, previous research has also raised a concern that NLU benchmarks are vulnerable to being manipulated by neural models. This makes it doubtful whether the performance metrics that neural models report on benchmark datasets are reliable and generalizable, and the NLU community has looked at this issue a lot. Researchers have tried different methods to reduce benchmark gaming so that NLU models show real language understanding. These include more comprehensive evaluation protocols, adversarial testing, and integrating external knowledge into training. But the first two do not change the training pipeline to make the model's language understanding better. The knowledge integration method does change the training procedure, but it is not clear whether the external knowledge is factually and sufficiently enforced in the integration.

We propose a new approach, the Recap, Deliberate, and Respond (RDR) paradigm, which deals with these limitations by putting three different objectives into the neural network pipeline. The first one is Recap, which paraphrases the input text with a dedicated model. This captures the essential and salient information of the input. The second one is Deliberate, and it encodes external graph information related to the entities that appear in the input text. It uses a graph embedding model to make use of the knowledge in the knowledge graphs. Because this external context is added into the pipeline, Deliberate improves the model's ability to understand relationships between entities and to extract relevant information for downstream tasks. The last objective is Respond, which uses a classification head model. This model takes the representations from the Recap and Deliberate modules and produces the final prediction. Since it uses what the Recap and Deliberate stages provide, Respond can make more accurate and informed predictions. The three objectives are cascaded and a combined loss is minimized, and this stops the model from artificially inflating performance metrics by exploiting statistical artifacts. Our method helps capture the true underlying semantic patterns of the input data with help from external knowledge, which leads to more reliable and accurate predictions.

To see if the RDR paradigm is effective, we test it on several GLUE benchmark tasks involving sentence similarity, textual entailment, and natural language inference. The results show better performance than competitive baselines, with improvements up to 2% on standard evaluation metrics. This shows that the RDR approach can improve the NLU performance of neural models. We also use inference examples from the RDR models to discuss how robust the model's semantic understanding is against statistical artifacts. We find that adding the Recap and Deliberate objectives leads to better comprehension of the underlying semantic patterns in the data and in the external knowledge.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Previous research in natural language understanding (NLU) and neural network pipelines has acknowledged the need to incorporate additional context beyond the input data [1]. To address this limitation, one well-established approach is to integrate external knowledge graphs as supplementary context [2]. Knowledge graphs contain structured information about entities, relationships, and concepts. This external information enables the neural network to infer semantic connections between entities, even when such relations are not explicitly stated in the data alone. The neural network is thus able to uncover implicit or missing contextual associations.

However, previous research has raised a notable concern about the vulnerability of NLU benchmarks to manipulation by neural models [3,4]. This casts doubt on the reliability and generalizability of the performance metrics neural models report on benchmark datasets, and the issue has been extensively scrutinized within the NLU community. Researchers have explored various methods to mitigate benchmark gaming so that NLU models exhibit authentic language understanding, including more comprehensive evaluation protocols, adversarial testing, and integrating external knowledge into training. However, the first two approaches do not redesign the training pipeline to enhance the model's language understanding. Although knowledge integration does modify the training procedure, it remains unclear whether the external knowledge is factually and sufficiently enforced in the integration process.

We propose a novel approach, the Recap, Deliberate, and Respond (RDR) paradigm, which addresses these limitations by integrating three distinct objectives within the neural network pipeline. The first objective, Recap, paraphrases the input text using a dedicated model, capturing the essential and salient information in the input. The second objective, Deliberate, encodes external graph information related to the entities that appear in the input text, using a graph embedding model to leverage the knowledge in the knowledge graphs. By integrating this external context into the pipeline, Deliberate enhances the model's capability to comprehend relationships between entities and extract relevant information for downstream tasks. The final objective, Respond, employs a classification head model that uses the representations from the Recap and Deliberate modules to generate the final prediction. By drawing on the Recap and Deliberate stages, Respond enables more accurate and informed predictions. The cascading structure of the three objectives, together with minimizing a combined loss, prevents the model from artificially inflating performance metrics by exploiting statistical artifacts. Our methodology thus captures the true underlying semantic patterns of the input data with the help of external knowledge, leading to more reliable and accurate predictions.

To evaluate the effectiveness of the RDR paradigm, we test our method on multiple GLUE benchmark tasks involving sentence similarity, textual entailment, and natural language inference [5,6,7,8,9]. The results show superior performance compared to competitive baselines, with improvements of up to 2% on standard evaluation metrics, highlighting the capability of the RDR approach to enhance the NLU performance of neural models. Furthermore, using inference examples from the RDR models, we discuss the model's robustness for semantic understanding against statistical artifacts. We find that introducing the Recap and Deliberate objectives leads to better comprehension of the underlying semantic patterns in both the data and the external knowledge.
